text: After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to see them,
and since they shared the same trade, he stayed and worked with them; they were tentmakers.

versions.text: and since they shared the same trade, he stayed with them and worked; they were tentmakers by trade.
versions.explanation: The repetition of "trade" within one short sentence is clumsy when read aloud. Dropping the second occurrence keeps the sense (the Greek explanatory clause simply identifies their craft) and improves the rhythm.

text: Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself entirely to the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
But when they opposed him and hurled abuse at him, he shook out his clothes and said to them, "Your blood is on your own heads. I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles."
So he left there and went into the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, came to believe in the Lord together with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.
One night the Lord said to Paul in a vision, "Do not be afraid. Keep on speaking; do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will lay a hand on you to harm you, because I have many people in this city."
So he settled there for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews joined together in an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat.
"This man," they said, "is persuading people to worship God in ways contrary to the law."
Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio said to the Jews, "If this were a matter of some crime or serious wrongdoing, you Jews, I would have good reason to hear you out.

versions.text: Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio said to the Jews, "If this were a matter of some crime or serious offense, I would have good reason to hear you out.
versions.explanation: The direct address ὦ Ἰουδαῖοι is left untranslated. Restoring it preserves the tone of Gallio's formal, somewhat dismissive ruling and matches the content of the Greek.

text: But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things."
And he drove them away from the judgment seat.
Then they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But none of this concerned Gallio in the least.

Paul stayed on in Corinth for many days. Then he said farewell to the brothers and sailed for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. Before sailing, he had his hair cut off at Cenchreae, because of a vow he had made.

versions.text: Paul stayed on in Corinth for some time. Then he said farewell to the brothers and sailed for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. Before sailing, he had his hair cut off at Cenchreae, because of a vow he had made.
versions.explanation: ἡμέρας ἱκανάς means "a considerable number of days"; "some time" understates the duration and loses the sense of an extended stay.

versions.text: Paul stayed on in Corinth for many days.
versions.explanation: Most of the verse was dropped: the farewell to the brothers (τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἀποταξάμενος), the voyage to Syria (ἐξέπλει εἰς τὴν Συρίαν), the companions Priscilla and Aquila, and the haircut at Cenchreae because of a vow (κειράμενος ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς τὴν κεφαλήν, εἶχεν γὰρ εὐχήν). The restored wording keeps the intentional change to "many days" and also supplies the antecedent for "the two of them" in the next verse.

text: They arrived at Ephesus, where he left the two of them. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay longer, he declined,
but as he said farewell he promised, "I will come back to you if God is willing." Then he set sail from Ephesus.
He landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he set out again and traveled from place to place through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and with burning enthusiasm he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
When he wanted to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On his arrival he was a great help to those who by grace had come to believe,
for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
